newsitem.title: USA: Too many stocks can spoil the fund.
newsitem.headline: Too many stocks can spoil the fund.

text.p: The typical equity mutual fund has more than 100 stocks in its portfolio, and some hold 1,000 or more.

The result, in many cases, is mediocre performance: after all, few managers can come up with 100 terrific stocks to buy. Thus, most stocks in a fund's portfolio aren't likely to add much value for shareholders.
If you want a manager's best ideas, and only those ideas, you need to find a fund with relatively few stocks in it.

Trouble is, that approach carries its own risks. Since most mutual fund managers lack the stock-picking skills of a Peter Lynch or Warren Buffett, you could end up with a fund that holds 15 or 20 rotten ideas. In that case, you'd be better off investing with a manager who simply buys a bushel of stocks, letting the law of averages cancel out his or her worst mistakes.

Meanwhile, many of the best stock-pickers in the fund industry have attracted droves of investors to their funds. Those managers have been forced to buy ever larger numbers of stocks to put assets to work. Result: more mediocrity.

What should you do? One solution is to resign yourself to investing in funds that will deliver average returns. In that case, it might make sense to invest a sizable portion of your savings in index funds -- funds that seek to mimic the performance of an index such as the Standard & Poor's 500.

A second strategy offers more hope of beating the market averages. It calls for seeking funds that over three to five years or longer have shown above-average gains given the risks they take. You'll find that those funds often hold 100 or more stocks, but their investments tend to be concentrated in selected sectors or types of firms.

For example, a fund at any moment might hold 30 of its 100 stocks in the technology sector and another 30 in financial services. The result could be gains -- or losses -- much greater than those of any index.

One example: Neuberger & Berman Genesis (800-877-9700; $1,000 minimum investment; no load). More than half of the fund's portfolio recently consisted of stocks in the energy and industrial sectors. The fund has posted around 47 percent higher returns that its typical competitor over the past three years, with about 20 percent less volatility.
Another solution: choose a fund that invests in a small number of stocks. Such funds are relatively rare, but some of them are managed by investors with a reputation for consistently picking winners.

One solid entry is Janus Twenty (800-525-8983; $2,500 minimum; no load), which holds a portfolio of 20 stocks that recently was concentrated in the financial and industrial cyclical sectors. Manager Tom Marsico looks for rapidly growing firms whose shares are selling at reasonable prices. That approach has helped the fund post a 15.9 percent annual return during the past 10 years, versus 12.8 percent for the typical large-company growth fund.

Another fund worth checking out is Clipper Fund (800-776-5033; $5,000 minimum; no load), which currently holds 19 stocks in its portfolio. The fund's managers look for large firms with valuable franchise operations trading at substantial discounts to their intrinsic values. Result: the fund has gained 19.2 percent annually during the past 5 years, vs. 14.6 percent for its typical competitor.

Finally, a new entry: the Yacktman Focus Fund (800-525-8258; $2,500 minimum; no load), which opened to investors on May 1. The fund will invest half of its portfolio in about 10 stocks and the other half in only five issues. Manager Donald Yacktman has compiled a distinguished record, first at Selected American Shares and then as founder of the Yacktman Fund. His approach calls for investing in quality companies when they trade at bargain prices -- and then patiently holding the shares until they recover.
Short-term investors will hate this fund: Yacktman is willing to ride out losses or accept subpar returns for months or even longer when he thinks a stock offers value.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
